records.text: The idea at work is a fork: one piece bearing down on several targets at once. Follow that one piece and see what it reaches.
All right. This leaves the other side a chance at a fork, with one piece able to reach several targets together. Find that piece first, then count what it could hit.
A different move offered a fork here, one piece reaching several targets at once. This move passes it by, so that is the comparison to make.
The idea here is a pin to the king. The pinned piece has to stay on its line, because stepping off would expose its own king.
This leaves the other side a chance to pin a piece to its king. Once pinned, that piece cannot leave the line without exposing the king. Find the line first.
A different move could have used a pin to the king. The pinned piece would have been stuck on its line, unable to move without exposing the king. That chance went by.
A skewer is at work. The attack meets the front piece first, and when it steps aside, the piece behind it is exposed on the same line.
This opens a skewer for the other side. If the front piece has to move, the piece behind it could be left exposed along that line. Check what sits behind it.
Another move offered a skewer. Moving the front piece would have exposed whatever stood behind it on the line. This move leaves that chance unused.
The idea is to capture a defender. Once it is gone, whatever it was guarding can lose its protection, so look at what depended on it.
This leaves the other side a chance to capture a defender. If that happens, what it was guarding could be left without protection. Start with what the defender holds.
A different move could have captured a defender and taken protection away from what it guarded. This move lets that chance pass. The defender's job is the place to begin.
There is a back-rank mating pattern here. The king's own pieces close off its escape, so the back rank is the place to look.
This gives the other side a route to a back-rank mate. The king is hemmed in by its own pieces, and that is the weakness to look at first.
There was a route to a back-rank mate, with the king boxed in by its own pieces. This move lets it slip by. That route is worth going back to.
Promotion is the aim. A pawn has a path to the last rank, where it can become a new piece. Follow that path one square at a time.
This gives the other side a chance to promote a pawn. Follow that pawn's path toward the last rank; that is the threat to keep in view.
A stronger move offered a path to promotion, and this one lets the chance go. Trace the pawn's route to the last rank and see what was there.
The idea is a discovered attack. One piece steps out of the way, and the piece behind it gets a clear line. Look at what that line reaches.
This opens a discovered attack for the other side. One of their pieces could step aside and uncover an attack from the piece behind it. Check which lines that would open.
Another move offered a discovered attack: move one piece aside and let the piece behind it do the attacking. This move does not use it.
Two threats arrive at the same time here; that is a double attack. Take each threat in turn, then see how they work together.
This leaves the other side a chance at a double attack, two threats at once. Both would need an answer, so look at them together rather than one by one.
A stronger move offered two attacks at once, and this move misses that. Lay the two threats out next to each other and the chance becomes clear.
This is a deflection. A defender is pulled away from its job, and what it was covering comes open. Find the job first, then the defender.
This gives the other side a chance at a deflection, drawing a defender away from its job. Look at what that defender is covering right now.
A different move could have drawn a defender away from its job. That deflection was available, and this move lets it pass. Start with what the defender was covering.
The idea is a plain one: an undefended piece can be taken. Loose pieces are always worth a look before anything more complicated.
Another move could have taken an undefended piece, and this one lets it go. A quick check for loose pieces is a good habit before settling on a move.
This leaves the other side a chance to take an undefended piece. Find the piece that has no protection; that is where to start.
Okay. This move takes away a piece's only effective defender, and now the other side can capture what was left behind. Before moving a defender, check what it was guarding.
The warning came with the opponent's last move. This move does not answer that threat, so a piece can now be captured. Begin with what their last move attacked.
This capture lets the other side recapture a more valuable piece. The first capture is only half of the trade; count both sides of the exchange.
This brings a minor piece off its starting square and into the game. Take a look at where it has settled.
Another move would have brought a minor piece off its starting square and into play. That is the difference to notice.
The rook now stands on an open file, a file with no pawns of either color on it.
Another move would have put a rook on an open file, with no pawns of either color along it.
The rook now sits on a semi-open file. None of its own pawns are there, but at least one enemy pawn still is.
A different move would have placed a rook on a semi-open file: no pawns of its own on it, though an enemy pawn remains.
This leaves a passed pawn. No enemy pawn stands ahead of it, either on its own file or on the files beside it.
Another move would have created a passed pawn, one with no enemy pawn in front of it on its file or the two beside it.
The pawn was already passed, and this move walks it forward. Compare where it stood with where it stands now.
Another move would have pushed the passed pawn forward. Have a look at where it could have gone.
This leaves an isolated pawn. There is no friendly pawn on either file beside it.
Another move would have left an isolated pawn, with no pawn of its own color on either neighboring file.
This gives a piece a defender it did not have before. It is no longer standing on its own.
Another move would have given an undefended piece some support, so it would not have been left by itself.
This leaves a piece undefended. That is worth noticing, though it does not mean the piece can actually be won.
Another move would have left a piece without a defender. On its own, that would not prove the piece could be won.
The king now has a legal flight square it did not have before. Compare the two positions to see what cleared the way.
Another move would have given the king a new square to step to. Look at what would have changed around it.
The king castles, and the rook comes across with it. Both pieces have moved, so follow each of them.
The alternative was to castle, moving the king and the rook together in a single turn.
With this capture, a bishop pair is gone. The side that lost the bishop is left without one for each square color.
A different move would have taken a bishop, leaving the other side without its pair.
This leaves doubled pawns, with pawns of the same color sharing one file.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, with pawns of the same color stacked on one file.
